0.0.n: A hesitation sound used while thinking about what to say.

0.2.n: The dish name combines 肉, meat, with a shortened form of じゃがいも, potato.

0.4.n: The speaker repeats the dish name before explaining it.

0.5.n: This ending gently invites the listener to follow along.

1.0.n: The dish is introduced as the topic of the explanation.

1.1.n: Marks 肉じゃが as what the speaker is talking about.

1.3.n: A filler that gives the speaker time to organize the explanation.

1.4.n: This first mention is part of a phrase the speaker abandons and restarts.

1.5.n: The speaker starts a linking phrase with の but abandons it before its role becomes clear.

1.6.n: This occurs in the hesitant opening before the speaker restarts with 牛肉と野菜.

1.8.n: The speaker repeats this ingredient to restart the list clearly.

1.9.n: Connects 牛肉 and 野菜 as the two ingredient groups.

1.10.n: Japanese nouns do not need a special plural ending.

1.11.n: A polite ending used after nouns to make a statement.

1.12.n: Softens the explanation and encourages shared understanding.

2.0.n: Written in katakana here; じゃがいも is also common.

2.2.n: Another ingredient in the list, written in katakana here.

2.4.n: The final ingredient in a list spoken without explicit connecting words.

2.5.n: Adds a friendly, conversational ending to the ingredient list.

3.0.n: A shortened version of the conversational filler まあ.

3.2.n: Introduces the aspect of the dish the speaker will describe next.

3.3.n: Marks 味 as the topic, shifting attention from ingredients to taste.

3.4.n: Names one of the seasonings used to explain the flavor.

3.5.n: Lists 醤油 as an example rather than giving a complete inventory.

3.7.n: A Japanese seasoning that adds sweetness to dishes.

3.8.n: Adds みりん as another example in the open-ended list.

3.9.n: Loosely links the seasoning list to the flavor description that follows.

3.11.n: Reduces the degree of 甘い, describing only mild sweetness.

3.12.n: An adjective describing the sweetness of the soy-sauce flavor.

3.13.n: Repeated here to identify the main flavor being described.

3.14.n: Connects 醤油 to 味 to specify what kind of taste it is.

3.15.n: The noun being compared with the dish’s overall flavor.

3.16.n: Follows a noun to express resemblance rather than exact identity.

3.17.n: Connects みたい to 感じ, which appears at the start of the next subtitle line.

4.0.n: Completes みたいな感じ from the preceding line, giving an approximate description.

4.2.n: Gives the description a gentle, conversational finish.

4.4.n: The name of a Japanese hot-pot dish, used here as a familiar flavor comparison.

4.5.n: Compares the taste to that of すき焼き.

4.6.n: Connects みたい to 味 so the comparison describes the taste.

4.7.n: Ends a shortened phrase with no explicit verb, which is natural in conversation.

0.lit: Um, meat-and-potato stew. Meat-and-potato stew, you know.
0.tip: ね gives the repeated dish name a friendly, listener-oriented tone.

1.lit: As for meat-and-potato stew, well, beef of—and, beef and vegetables, you know.
1.tip: The speaker stumbles over 牛肉のと, then restarts clearly with 牛肉と野菜.

2.tip: Spoken Japanese can list ingredients with pauses instead of saying と between every item.

3.lit: Well, as for flavor, of soy sauce and mirin and such, like a slightly sweet soy-sauce taste…
3.tip: とか lists examples, implying these are seasonings rather than necessarily the complete list.

4.lit: An impression it is, you know. A taste like sukiyaki.
4.tip: みたいな before a noun means that noun resembles something: すき焼きみたいな味 is a taste like sukiyaki.
